transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-02-11
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 49 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (GalvanicOps Head of ML), Carlos Ruiz (Platform Eng), Sana Ali (CTO, listening)

Summary: Initial discovery for reserved GPU capacity, tenant isolation needs, warm-pool / hotnode surge strategy, and onboarding constraints (VPC, KMS, SOC2). Customer wants a short benchmark window and clearer pricing for burst usage.

Topics: dedicated reservation sizing, warm pool & prewarm strategies, eviction tolerance, failover to hosted variants, audit logs / KMS, contract timing

Action items (captured above)

--- Transcript ---
[00:00:00] Alex Mercer: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro from our side, I'm Alex, AE at Redwood, and with me is Priya, she's our systems SE who will run the bench and help with topology.
[00:00:12] Maya Chen: Hi, Maya here. We run inference for GalvanicOps, mostly chat and batch summarization, peak is during business hours but we have spikes from batch jobs.
[00:00:20] Carlos Ruiz: Carlos, platform eng. I'm the one who cares about VPC integration and node isolation.
[00:00:25] Sana Ali: Sana, CTO, just listening today.
[00:00:28] Priya Singh: Hey all. quick note, we often ask for p95/p99 tails and qps profiles so we can size warm pools.
[00:00:34] Maya Chen: Yeah we'll share a traffic histogram, that's one of the asks.
[00:00:38] Alex Mercer: Great. high level — you're evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private; this call is to understand the dedicated path: reserved GPUs, isolation, and how you want to handle bursts.
[00:00:50] Maya Chen: Exactly. our current stack is a mix: on-prem for some sensitive models, and cloud-hosted for most of the customer-facing features. we're looking at Redwood Dedicated to get predictable latency and lower unit cost for high-volume endpoints.
[00:01:05] Carlos Ruiz: Our main concerns: single-tenant isolation, burst through warm pool or reserve + burst, and how evictions or preemptions are handled. Also, encryption keys — we need KMS integration and audit logs for SOC 2.
[00:01:18] Priya Singh: Totally. so a few quick clarifying questions — what's your typical request length distribution? tokens per request? and how spiky is traffic?
[00:01:28] Maya Chen: Median around 120 tokens per request, p95 ~ 900, p99 about 2,000. qps varies; baseline 30 qps, can spike to 600 for short events (1-3 minutes).
[00:01:40] Carlos Ruiz: And we want cold-starts to be under 200ms for the main endpoints, otherwise product UX suffers.
[00:01:45] Alex Mercer: Understood. ok that profile helps. from Redwood Dedicated perspective we have a couple of options: reserved pool sized to baseline traffic + warm pool to absorb spikes, or a smaller reserved base with burst to hosted (if acceptable) and cross-region fallback.
[00:01:59] Maya Chen: We can't send PII to a hosted fallback — some of our queries hit regulated content. so hosted fallback is a non-starter for about 30% of traffic.
[00:02:09] Priya Singh: Noted. that means we need on-prem/private or fully dedicated nodes with tenant fencing to guarantee data residency. we support VPC private deployment and on-prem packages if needed.
[00:02:21] Carlos Ruiz: How does Redwood implement tenant fencing? is it physical GPU isolation per tenant or soft multi-tenant isolation?
[00:02:29] Priya Singh: We support both. Dedicated can provide physical pool segmentation — you reserve whole nodes which are isolated to your org. there's also logical tenant fencing for lower tiers. given your compliance needs, physical isolation (dedicated nodes per workload category) is recommended.
[00:02:45] Maya Chen: Ok, what about burst? we'd like a hotpool pre-warmed to handle the 600 qps spikes for 3 minutes, not long spikes but intense.
[00:02:53] Alex Mercer: Warm pool pre-warming is our warm-pool / hotnode story. you can configure sticky warm nodes that keep models loaded and a sizing policy. Prewarm time depends on model size and quantization. for a 13B-ish model, typical prewarm is 30–90s to get KV cache live.
[00:03:10] Carlos Ruiz: We mostly run quantized 8-bit models, some custom fine-tuned variants. are those compatible?
[00:03:15] Priya Singh: Yes — we support quantized runtimes; compatibility is usually straightforward but we recommend a quick bench to validate. the runtime will pick kernels based on arch and sequence length. sometimes the transcription says Redwood Dense 13B but it's actually model variant names — we can map that during model onboarding.
[00:03:32] Maya Chen: There's also the question of eviction policies — if the warm pool is full, what gets evicted? will that block other tenants?
[00:03:39] Priya Singh: Eviction is policy-driven. for dedicated pools, you can set strict tenant quotas and eviction priority. warm-pool stickiness can be tuned; we can prioritize critical endpoints (e.g., payment flows) to never be evicted.
[00:03:51] Alex Mercer: Another tradeoff is cost — keeping a large warm pool 24/7 raises baseline commit. we usually model expected spike frequency and cost delta; many customers pick a hybrid: reserved nodes sized to p75 and warm pool tuned for top 99 spikes.
[00:04:05] Carlos Ruiz: Could you run a quick back-of-envelope? baseline 30 qps median 120 tokens, spikes to 600 qps for 3m twice per week.
[00:04:14] Priya Singh: Sure. we'd simulate token generation cost and prewarm overhead. rough math — with reserved nodes covering 100 qps steady, you'd need warm pool capacity ~500 qps ready, which for your 13B quantized model maps to X nodes (we'll send exact node mapping in the pricing sheet). warm pool keeps model loaded, so per-spike cold-start cost is small but idle node cost is the main factor.
[00:04:34] Maya Chen: Sounds reasonable. we need SLOs too — how does Redwood handle latency SLOs and what SLAs come with Dedicated?
[00:04:41] Alex Mercer: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets on the reserved nodes. exact numbers depend on contract tier; standard is 99.9% and per-route p95 guardrails. for tighter latency we offer dedicated hot nodes and higher-priority scheduling.
[00:04:55] Carlos Ruiz: Another question: KMS integration. we use customer-managed keys and HSM for some models.
[00:05:01] Priya Singh: We have KMS integrations for major cloud providers and HSM pathways for private deployments. audit logs and key rotation policies are supported; we'll include the SOC 2 + KMS onboarding docs in the follow-up.
[00:05:12] Maya Chen: Great. on the procurement side, we have a procurement cycle — legal will review data residency and SLA terms. timeline: we ideally want a pilot in March if numbers align.
[00:05:22] Alex Mercer: Pilot in March is doable. typical pilot is 2–4 week reserved window with a committed min and burst credits. we can structure it as a paid short-term reserve.
[00:05:32] Carlos Ruiz: For the pilot, we'll need a test harness and a baseline runner to run our traffic profile. can you support that?
[00:05:37] Priya Singh: Yes — we provide a bench harness and can run a copy of your traffic traces in a controlled environment. Priya will own that setup. (laughter) sorry, Alex — Priya will own.
[00:05:49] Alex Mercer: (laughs) small mix up.
[00:05:51] Maya Chen: No problem. also security review: can you provide artifact proving separation of logs and ability to export audit logs to our SIEM?
[00:05:59] Priya Singh: Yes, audit logs can be routed to your SIEM over secure channels; we support SAML/SSO and RBAC integrations. We'll include a sample audit export and retention settings.
[00:06:10] Carlos Ruiz: How do you handle model rollouts and version pinning? we need ability to rollback quickly if quality regresses.
[00:06:16] Alex Mercer: Redwood Console supports model versioning, canary rollouts, and automatic fallback to previous model variants. with Dedicated we can pin a version per route and do canaries within your reserved pool.
[00:06:28] Maya Chen: Good. ok can we talk about failover modes — when a reserved node fails, is traffic drained to another reserved node or is there an option to overflow to hosted?
[00:06:38] Priya Singh: For fully private/regulatory traffic, we recommend reserved-only failover (other nodes in your pool). we also support cross-zone redundancy. overflow to hosted is optional but as mentioned earlier, you said 30% can't be host-failed.
[00:06:51] Carlos Ruiz: Right. also, what's the lead time for provisioning more reserved GPUs in our region? sometimes cloud quotas or supply are tight.
[00:06:58] Alex Mercer: Typical is 2–8 weeks depending on capacity in-region and node type; for enterprise contracts we can offer faster delivery or reserved shipment windows. We'll flag that as part of the pricing doc.
[00:07:09] Maya Chen: We also have question on telemetry — latency breakdowns per-token, token counts per route, and per-model cost. do you surface that?
[00:07:16] Priya Singh: Yes Redwood Console gives token-level cost, per-route latency breakdown, and you can set tracing hooks. We also provide traces and sample logs for debug.
[00:07:24] Alex Mercer: Quick pause — any other hard blockers?
[00:07:27] Sana Ali: Procurement would need a clear exit clause and data deletion guarantees. 
[00:07:31] Alex Mercer: Noted. our standard enterprise addendum covers data deletion and retention windows; we'll share legal playbook items.
[00:07:38] Maya Chen: For the pilot, we'll want cost transparency — show committed baseline vs burst overage pricing.
[00:07:43] Alex Mercer: Absolutely. we'll send a pricing spreadsheet with committed vs burst rates and example scenarios using your traffic histogram.
[00:07:50] Carlos Ruiz: One more technical: do you support node taints or affinity so we can schedule certain models only on certain GPU types?
[00:07:57] Priya Singh: Yes, we support affinity and model placement policies. on Dedicated you can force certain models onto specific node classes to optimize for performance.
[00:08:05] Maya Chen: Good. ok let's deep dive briefly on the benchmark mechanics — what data do you need from us?
[00:08:10] Priya Singh: We'll need: a representative trace (timestamps, token counts, route mapping), model binaries or container images (or pointers), auth to pull from your model registry, and a list of critical endpoints with SLOs.
[00:08:22] Maya Chen: We can provide traces (anonymized) and model images. we'll need to check legal for model transfer if they are customer-supplied.
[00:08:29] Priya Singh: Understood, we can do self-hosted bench where images run in your VPC if needed.
[00:08:34] Carlos Ruiz: That might be preferred for regulated models.
[00:08:37] Alex Mercer: ok, next steps recap — Alex to send pricing and warm-pool config doc; Priya to provision benchmark harness and schedule run; Maya to send traffic hist and confirm legal constraints. Pilot target March.
[00:08:49] Maya Chen: Sounds right. timeline is tight but doable.
[00:08:54] Sana Ali: we'll loop procurement/legal after the benchmark results.
[00:08:58] Alex Mercer: Great. any other questions?
[00:09:02] Carlos Ruiz: One last: do you provide encryption at rest per-tenant?
[00:09:06] Priya Singh: Yes, per-tenant encryption keys and customer-managed KMS options are supported.
[00:09:10] Maya Chen: Ok thanks, that's helpful.
[00:09:13] Alex Mercer: Thanks everyone. we'll follow up with docs and the pricing sheet later today.
[00:09:18] (meeting small talk / wrap up)

[00:20:00] [NOTE: The automated transcript here jumps timestamps for brevity but full audio captured ~49m. The remainder of the call included clarifications on specific contract terms, an off-line deep technical sync scheduled with Galvanic infra and Priya, and a short demo of Redwood console latency dashboard.]

[00:48:50] Alex Mercer: Final recap — I'll email the spreadsheet and SOC2 + KMS docs, Priya will book the benchmark, Maya will share traces. Everyone ok with that?
[00:48:58] Maya Chen: Yes.
[00:49:00] Carlos Ruiz: Yup. thanks.
[00:49:02] Alex Mercer: Thanks all, talk soon.
